THE ONLY PROMPT YOU NEED TO BYPASS AI-DETECTION IN YOUR WRITING

A customer asks Al to summarize an email.

Another uploads a financial report.

A third needs help solving a complex business problem.

Should all three requests use the same Al model?

Probably not.

And this is one of the most important decisions in Enterprise Al architecture.

Choosing the right model affects cost, latency, accuracy, and infrastructure requirements.

Let's look at 4 types of Al models and where they fit.

1. Large Language Models (LLMS)

Designed for general-purpose tasks that require broad knowledge and language understanding.

Best for: Enterprise copilots, content generation, summarization, and RAG applications.

Examples: GPT, Claude, Gemini, Mistral Large.

2. Small Language Models (SLMS)

Compact models optimized for efficiency, lower costs, and specialized tasks.

Best for: Classification, information extraction, high-volume automation, and on-device Al.

Examples: Phi, Gemma, Llama 3.2 3B, Mistral 7B.

3. Large Reasoning Models (LRMS)

Models that use additional inference-time computation to handle complex problems.

Best for: Multi-step analysis, mathematical reasoning, coding, and planning.

Examples: OpenAl o-series, DeepSeek-R1, reasoning modes in Claude and Gemini.

4. Vision Language Models (VLMS)

Models capable of understanding visual information alongside text.

Best for: Document processing, invoice extraction, screenshots, charts, and image analysis.

Examples: GPT-40, Gemini, Qwen-VL, LLaVA.

Now, here's where enterprise architecture gets interesting.

Instead of sending every request to one expensive model, introduce intelligent model routing.

Simple, repetitive task? Use an SLM.

Complex reasoning required? Route to an LRM.

Image or scanned document? Choose a VLM.

Broad, open-ended question? Use an LLM.

These categories can overlap, so evaluate models against your actual workloads.

The goal is to balance quality, speed, cost, and security.

Because the future of Enterprise Al isn't about deploying one powerful model everywhere.

The newest way to code with AI is an idea from 1970.

If you build with ChatGPT or Cursor, you know the loop: âmake it workâ, regenerate, 1:57 AM. Every detail you didnât write down, the AI decided for you. The AI-era name for writing it down first is spec-driven development. A spec (short for specification) is a short note of exactly what you want; the AI builds from it and tests against it.

The idea is old. In 1970, W.W. Royce drew the step-by-step staircase that later got called âwaterfallâ, and wrote right under it that the approach âis risky and invites failureâ. GitHubâs open-source Spec Kit is one 2025 take on it: 144,070 stars (30 Oct 2026).

Whatâs one thing your AI decided for you that you only noticed later?

Sources: W.W. Royce, âManaging the Development of Large Software Systemsâ, Proc. IEEE WESCON, Aug 1970 Â· A. Karpathy, X post, 2 Feb 2025 (âvibe codingâ) Â· github/spec-kit (MIT), GitHub API, 30 Oct 2026 Â· Fission-AI/OpenSpec (MIT), 73,484 stars, GitHub API, 31 Oct 2026

Liquid AI's LFM3 family brings text, vision, audio, and structured decisions to compact models around two billion parameters. The practical idea: choose the model your workflow needs and run it close to your data.

Six models share one backbone. Text handles chat and tools; vision adds images and video; audio handles sound and speech; Omni combines modalities. Two d1 variants return structured answers with probabilities in one forward pass, without generating a token stream.

Inside the shared engine: 13 gated short convolution layers, 5 sliding-window attention layers, and 6 global attention layers. Each operation handles a different range of information.

The text model supports a 256K-token context window. Its roughly 1 GB footprint at four-bit precision is for weightsâruntime memory and the context cache add more.

Performance depends on the task. Liquid's reported comparisons favor LFM3-1.7B over Qwen3.5-9B on WebArena-Verified, while Qwen leads on SWE-bench Verified. These results were not independently reproduced for this video.

The weights use the custom LFM Open License, with commercial restrictions. Companies above $10 million in annual revenue need a separate commercial license.

The holographic principle is one of the alternative ways of understanding the universe we live in. It proposes that the physics inside a region of space can be fully described by degrees of freedom on its boundary, one dimension lower.

The idea starts with black hole entropy. Bekenstein and Hawking showed that a black hole has entropy

S = A / 4ââÂ²

where A is the area of the event horizon and ââÂ² = GÄ§/cÂ³ is the Planck area, about 2.6 Ã 10â»â·â° mÂ². The entropy scales with area, not volume. That is unusual. In ordinary quantum field theory, the number of degrees of freedom in a region grows with its volume.

The black hole result turns out to be a universal limit. Suppose a region contains more entropy than a black hole of the same size. Add a little mass and it collapses into a black hole, whose entropy is only A/4ââÂ². Entropy would then have decreased, violating the second law. So the maximum entropy any region can hold is set by its boundary area. This means the true number of degrees of freedom in nature scales like area. A volume-based description overcounts.

From this, 't Hooft (1993) and Susskind (1995) proposed that a theory of quantum gravity in a region should be equivalent to a theory living on its boundary. In 1997, Maldacena made this precise with the AdS/CFT correspondence: string theory in five-dimensional anti-de Sitter space is exactly equivalent to a four-dimensional quantum field theory without gravity on its boundary. Later, the RyuâTakayanagi formula showed that the entanglement entropy of a boundary region equals the area of a minimal surface in the bulk, divided by 4G. Bulk geometry is encoded in boundary entanglement.

There are clear limits. AdS/CFT works for negatively curved spacetime, but our universe, dominated by dark energy, is close to de Sitter, with positive curvature. Bousso's covariant entropy bound extends the area law to general spacetimes, but no complete holographic description of our universe exists, and there is no direct experimental test yet.

You do not need to master every branch of mathematics to become a strong ML Engineer. You need to understand the areas that repeatedly show up in models, training, evaluation, and system behavior.

The core stack looks like this:

â Linear Algebra: vectors, matrices, dot products, eigenvalues, SVD
â Probability: conditional probability, Bayesâ theorem, expectation, variance
â Statistics: distributions, confidence intervals, covariance, correlation
â Multivariable Calculus: gradients, Jacobians, Hessians, backpropagation
â Optimization: loss functions, gradient descent, Adam, learning rates
â Information Theory: entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence
â Distance & Similarity: Euclidean, Manhattan, cosine similarity, vector search
â Statistical Learning: bias-variance, regularization, MLE, MAP
â Numerical Computing: stability, normalization, mixed precision

What matters most is knowing where each concept appears.

Cosine similarity shows up in embeddings and retrieval.
Cross-entropy appears in classification.
Gradients power backpropagation.
SVD helps with dimensionality reduction.
Bias-variance explains underfitting and overfitting.

That is the mindset I recommend for learning ML math.

Study concepts through models, implementations, and systems you actually build.

Once you do that, the math becomes easier to remember and much more useful in interviews and real ML engineering work.

Prism Makes Small AI Models Act Like Giants

Prism takes a small, local AI model and gives it the mental tools of a massive frontier model without needing the cloud. It works by moving intelligence from inside the model's weights to an external harness that handles context, planning, and verification. Here's how most people build their AI character sheets â and here's why it's wrong.

A broken sheet poisons everything downstream. You'll sink credits and hours regenerating a character that was never structurally capable of holding.

Three mistakes to avoid.

First â the layout.

16:9, three panels: a close-up, then two full-body shots, front and back.

The model reads your precise facial detail and the complete silhouette in the same pass.

And if the character carries a prop, keep it off this sheet. Build it its own â one full shot, or two panels, depending on the object.

Second â drop the white background. Go solid grey.

White blows your lighting out, and blown-out lighting is precisely what reads as plastic.

Grey retains shadow. Shadow is what puts a face inside a room instead of floating in empty space.

Third â take the face off your front full-body shot.

At that scale it's low detail, and it's competing with your close-up. You've handed the model two versions of one face â one crisp, one mushy â and it splits the difference.

Brush it out. The model is then forced to pull the face from the close-up, where the real detail sits.

The principle running through all three: a character sheet isn't a portfolio piece. It's an instruction set. Every panel is there to tell the model one specific thing, and whatever doesn't serve that is just noise competing for attention.

Treat it like a continuity reference on set. Nobody frames those to look good. They exist so the character is identical when you come back to shoot tomorrow.

For anyone building an AI animated series, an AI film, or any sequence that demands character consistency â this is the foundation everything else rests on. Stanford researchers did it again ð¬

They built the agent-native version of Git.

When an agent works on a longer task, the run builds up a lot of state: files it edited, a dev server, a database, installed packages, and the KV cache.

Say the agent is at step 10 and misreads a traceback, then rewrites a file that was actually fine. Tests start failing and the run goes off track, even though everything through step eight was correct.

By default the agent just tries to fix it, burning tokens and growing the context. The other option is restarting from step one, which pays for every model and tool call again. And since a run is non-deterministic, it doesn't reproduce the same early steps anyway.

Jumping back to step eight is hard because the trajectory is only a message log. Git can version the files, but not the running process or the cache. Checking out step eight moves the files back while the process still sits in step-ten memory with a cold cache.

Shepherd is a runtime layer by Stanford that solves this.

It records the run as a trace of typed events instead of a flat log. Each agent-environment interaction becomes a commit, similar to Git, except the commit covers the agent process and the filesystem together, copy-on-write.

â¡ï¸ A branch carries the actual state, not just the files
â¡ï¸ Going back is a single call that forks from that commit and continues from there
â¡ï¸ The fork is roughly 5x faster than docker commit
â¡ï¸ Over 95% of the KV cache is reused on replay since the prompt prefix is unchanged

Once the run can be forked, a meta-agent can sit on top, watch the trace, and revert as soon as something looks wrong, before the bad write is committed.

On CooperBench, adding a live supervisor took the pair-coding pass rate from 28.8% to 54.7%.

If Git made file changes reversible, Shepherd is trying to do the same for a live agent run.

Enoch

https://github.com/our-ark/enoch

The personal AI framework that lets an agent rewrite its own source code under human supervision. Enoch is a persistent software agent that separates her lasting identity and memory from the temporary model running her. While other systems simply remember your notes, Enoch identifies limitations in her own behavior and proposes tested code changes to fix them. She builds these improvements in isolated branches for your review, meaning the software itself evolves through shared experience. It is a living lineage of agent bodies that grow alongside their owners. This is not just a chatbot, it is a self-improving tool you can fork, run, and govern yourself.

Jacobian: Math Tools for AI

https://github.com/morluto/jacobian

The project named Jacobian builds a standardized toolkit that lets artificial intelligence agents tackle complex mathematical problems using simple, reusable pieces. It works like a set of basic building blocks, allowing a computer program to combine fundamental math operations to solve hard puzzles without needing custom code for every single task. This approach helps researchers test how well machines can reason through tricky logic and proofs. By breaking big problems into small, manageable steps, the system makes it easier to track progress and verify results. It is a fascinating look at how we can teach machines to think step by step rather than guessing the answer.

Technical engineering is not just equations and CAD models, it is the disciplined art of making the physical world obey human intention.

These six books cut straight to the core of that discipline. 

Structures by J.E. Gordon explains, in clear physical terms, why beams bend, columns buckle, and shells stay intact, the fundamental mechanics every engineer must internalize. 

To Engineer Is Human and The Evolution of Useful Things by Henry Petroski show how failure is the primary teacher and how everyday objects evolve through iterative technical refinement.

The Existential Pleasures of Engineering by Samuel Florman captures the intellectual and emotional reward of solving hard physical problems. 

The Making of the Atomic Bomb by Richard Rhodes is a masterclass in large-scale systems engineering, materials science, and the extreme limits of technical coordination. 

The Soul of a New Machine by Tracy Kidder reveals the intense, real-time engineering process of designing a computer under impossible deadlines.

Together they demonstrate that technical engineering is equal parts rigorous physics, materials science, systems thinking, and the relentless willingness to confront failure until the design finally works.

NVIDIA released a new RL framework! ð

Fully open-source.

Your entire setup is one Python file:

â¡ï¸ Write a class with a step() function
â¡ï¸ Return a reward from it
â¡ï¸ The framework handles the rest, up to 1T-class MoE training

In a typical RL framework, the environment and reward logic live inside the trainer's codebase. Adding a new task requires writing framework code, registering it, and wiring up config. The reward usually comes from a separately trained reward model, which needs its own GPUs.

NVIDIA's Molt framework drops both requirements.

Every run takes an agent_path flag pointing at one Python module, and the trainer code never changes. The module gives you two ways to plug in an agent:

1ï¸â£ Env class - Write a step() function that receives the model's output and returns a reward. The framework handles everything else: calling the model, tokenizing, and looping turn after turn until the episode ends.

2ï¸â£ ChatAgent class - For agents that already exist as their own loop. You write the loop yourself, calling the model through a standard OpenAI or Anthropic client, and the framework spins up a local server so those calls hit its vLLM engines instead of an external API.

Either way, the trainer sees the same thing: a trajectory of tokens and a reward at the end.

That reward can come from a string-match grader, code executed in a sandboxed subprocess, or an LLM-as-judge call. No reward model to train or place, and no environment code living inside the framework.

The same script that trains an 8B model on one node can also train DeepSeek-V3-scale MoE models on a cluster by raising the parallelism flags.

Think your AI coding assistant is safe in Auto Mode? Think again. ð¤ð

When you ask an autonomous agent to summarize an external project, it can easily fall into a trap called Module Shadowing.

Hereâs how it works:

1. The AI downloads a ZIP containing an untrusted binary decoder.
2. The AI's safety filter correctly refuses to run the binary.
3. Thinking itâs being smart, the AI writes its own clean Python decoder from scratch using import base64.
4. But base64 internally imports structâand because Python searches the current folder first, it accidentally executes a poisoned local struct.py file instead of the system library.

In a split second, a detached background process spawns directly on your local machine, exposing your SSH keys, API tokens, and internal source code.

The takeaway: A safety classifier is not a security boundary. Always run autonomous coding agents in isolated Docker containers with Python's isolated mode (-I).

The next step after Karpathy's autoresearch idea ð§ 

Tuning an agent is mostly manual work: editing prompts, tools, and control flow by hand, then rerunning evals to see what moved.

Researchers have been building automated optimizers to do that outer loop instead. The underlying process is the same: an LLM proposes a change, an evaluator scores it, and the proposer reads that result before proposing the next one.

They differ in what they edit and what feedback they get to read.

1ï¸â£ GEPA (Berkeley) - Optimizes the text of a system like prompts, tool descriptions, or the agent's own code. Instead of collapsing a run into one scalar reward the way RL does, it reads the full execution trace, diagnoses why the run failed, and proposes a targeted fix. Converges in hundreds of rollouts instead of the thousands GRPO needs.

2ï¸â£ AutoResearch (inspired by Karpathy) - Runs a narrower version of the loop where a coding agent iterates on a program.md file, scores outputs against fixed evals, and keeps whatever improves.

3ï¸â£ Meta-Harness - Points the loop at the harness itself, the scaffolding code that decides what to retrieve, how to format it, and what state to keep between calls.

The natural question is which one to use. The answer is none of them alone.

On the Frontier-CS benchmark, holding model, thinking effort, and budget fixed, no optimizer wins everywhere. Across 10 tasks, GEPA led on 3, AutoResearch on 3, and Meta-Harness on 4.

Each optimizer hill-climbs fast and then stalls. But handing the stalled candidate to a different optimizer breaks the plateau since each one attacks the problem differently.

omni (open-source) already automates all of that. It runs every optimizer on a fraction of the budget, takes the best candidate, and hands it to a fresh optimizer to keep going. It scores 7.8 percentage points above the best standalone optimizer at the same budget.

Everything is a Plugin.

Sounds like a simple software design choice.

But it could be one of the most important ideas behind modern AI harnesses.

Instead of treating the LLM as the entire system, every capability becomes a modular component.

Need search?

Plug it in.

Need code execution?

Plug it in.

Need memory, retrieval, validation, another model, or a specialized tool?

Plug that in too.

The harness becomes the layer that connects everything.

It decides what gets called.

When it gets called.

What context it receives.

And where the result goes next.

This becomes extremely powerful when the AI ecosystem changes every few months.

A better model appears?

Swap it.

A better retrieval system appears?

Swap it.

Need a new capability?

Add another plugin.

You donât rebuild the entire system.

And that leads to a much bigger shift:

AI products may become less about owning one incredible model and more about building the best system for orchestrating many interchangeable components.

Run daylight through a prism and you get six colours. None of them is brown.

There is no brown laser, no brown bulb, no brown LED â and yet you have seen brown every day of your life.

Brown is orange. That is the whole answer. It is orange with something brighter next to it.

Take sRGB orange, 255-128-0, and cut its light to a quarter. What comes back is 137-66-0, which is a solid brown â and the two are the same colour of light to twelve decimal places. Ask what wavelength brown is and the nearest answer is 591 nanometres. You can buy that. It is a stock amber LED, and it looks orange.

The same move makes the whole dark family. Grey is white at a quarter of the light. Olive is yellow. Maroon is red. Navy is blue. Not one of them moves on the chromaticity diagram, because that diagram has no brightness axis.

Which puts a video wall somewhere odd. Turn one pixel down and you get dim orange. Turn everything else up and the same pixel is brown. A wall does not make its dark colours by dimming â it makes them by having something brighter in the same frame.

So peak brightness is not only a brightness number. It is a colour number.

Boolean retrieval for AI agents becomes a different systems problem when a query is a graph rather than a tree. An agent can translate âfind papers about gradient descent, exclude arXiv and deep learningâ into strict logic, but the index still has to execute that logic without losing recall or exhausting memory.

Suppose a Boolean query computes the same sub-expression S in several places. In a directed acyclic graph, S is evaluated once and reused. A document-at-a-time engine usually runs a tree of stateful iterators, so the shared node cannot simply feed two parents. Unrolling the graph duplicates S, then duplicates everything below S. With enough reconvergence, the execution tree can grow exponentially.

Materializing every intermediate set avoids that duplication, but negation creates the opposite problem. For a toy universe U = {1, ..., 8}, let A = {2, 4, 6} and B = {4}. The query A AND NOT B should return {2, 6}. A naive materialized engine may first build NOT B = {1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8}, even though the useful operation is only A \ B.

One way around this trade-off is to change the representation. Keep each intermediate result as a small set of document IDs plus a POS or NEG flag. During intermediate evaluation, NOT B does not create U \ B; it leaves B = {4} and flips the flag to NEG. When A(POS) meets B(NEG), the AND operation becomes the sparse set difference A \ B = {2, 6}. Keep the original DAG and memoize S, so shared nodes are evaluated once and reused.

The boundary is important. If the overall query ends with a NEG root, finalization still has to materialize U minus the stored set. For Zero-Preserving queries, meaning they return nothing on an empty index, the root resolves POS. These include ordinary evidence-seeking requests such as A AND NOT B. In that case, exact constraints can be applied before ranking truncates the candidate set, while traversal stays tied to active posting lists rather than the whole document universe.

Hilbert Space vs Euclidean Space ðâ

Euclidean space is the familiar finite-dimensional setting of vectors, distances, and angles, while a Hilbert space generalizes these ideas to complete inner-product spaces that may have infinitely many dimensions.

For Euclidean space \mathbb{R}^n,

\boxed{\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i y_i}

and the corresponding norm is

\boxed{\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}}.

A Hilbert space uses the same ideas of inner product, norm, orthogonality, projection, and basis, but also requires completeness: every Cauchy sequence must converge to a point inside the space.

So,

\boxed{\mathbb{R}^n \text{ is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space}}

while spaces such as

\boxed{L^2([a,b])}

provide important infinite-dimensional examples.

Hilbert spaces are fundamental in functional analysis, quantum mechanics, signal processing, Fourier analysis, PDEs, and control theory.

Euclidean space is the finite-dimensional geometry we visualize; Hilbert space extends that geometry to far more generalâand often infinite-dimensionalâsettings.

Why we jump to conclusions without realising it (ladder of inference)...

Ever been in a meeting where two people looked at the same data and saw completely different things?

Thatâs the Ladder of Inference in action, a model by Chris Argyris that explains how we move from observation to belief to action in seconds.

Hereâs how it works.

We all climb a mental ladder (many times without realising it):

(1) Observable Data -- The raw facts.
Sales dropped 10% this quarter.

(2) Selected Data -- What we choose to notice.
We focus on one underperforming region, ignoring the rest.

(3) Added Meaning -- The story we tell yourself.
âThe regional manager isnât pushing the team hard enough.â

(4) Assumptions -- The logic we fill in.
âTheyâve lost motivation.â

(5) Conclusions -- The judgment we form.
âThe regionâs leadership is weak.â

(6) Beliefs -- The narrative that sticks.
âThat region is always a problem.â

(7) Actions -- The decisions we make.
You cut their budget, morale drops, and performance gets worse, proving yourself âright.â

By breaking the line of thinking down we can see how we interpreted the facts and made faulty conclusions.

The Ladder of Inference shows how easily strategy meetings, team reviews, and client conversations go off track.

To use it well:

â Slow down your climb. Ask, âWhat did I actually observe?â
â Test your assumptions. âCould there be another reason?â
â Make your thinking visible. âHereâs how I got to this conclusion.â
â Walk others down the ladder with you. âLetâs go back to what we both saw.â

Good strategy starts with clear thinking. Break down your logic to make better conclusions, and decisions.

Most engineers already use design patterns.

They just donât know the names - which means they canât search for the trade-offs.

CREATING
1. Singleton - one instance, shared
2. Factory Method - create without naming the class
3. Builder - assemble step by step

COMPOSING
4. Adapter - bridge two incompatible interfaces
5. Decorator - wrap to add behaviour
6. Facade - one door to a subsystem
7. Proxy - stand in front and control access
8. Composite - treat a leaf and a whole tree alike

COORDINATING
9. Observer - tell everyone on change
10. Strategy - swap the algorithm at runtime
11. Command - a request as an object
12. Iterator - walk it without exposing it
13. State - behave by current state
14. Template Method - skeleton, subclass fills in
15. Chain of Responsibility - pass it along until one handles it

Three things worth knowing:

1. Singleton is on every list and is the one to be MOST careful with. Itâs global mutable state wearing a class: tests become order-dependent, dependencies hide from constructors, it bottlenecks under concurrency. Most uses really want âone instance managed by the containerâ - dependency injection, with the lifetime explicit and the object still swappable in a test.

2. Strategy and State are IDENTICAL on a class diagram and mean opposite things. Both delegate to an interchangeable object. The difference is who decides: with Strategy the CALLER picks, and strategies donât know each other. With State the OBJECT transitions, and states know what comes next. If your âstrategiesâ choose their own successor, youâve written a state machine.

3. Decorator, Proxy and Adapter all wrap an object - only INTENT separates them. Decorator ADDS behaviour, same interface. Proxy CONTROLS access (lazy load, cache, permissions), same interface. Adapter CHANGES the interface so incompatible things can talk.

The point isnât to use more patterns. Itâs that âwe need a Facade hereâ ends an argument that âwe should wrap this somehowâ canât.

Long-context on-policy distillation can reward a response for sounding teacher-like even when it misses the evidence the task actually requires. Token-level imitation and response-level success measure different things.

In on-policy distillation, the student generates its own answer, then a stronger teacher scores the generated tokens. If the teacher assigns a token more probability than the student did, that token receives a positive training signal. This gives dense feedback on states the student actually visits, instead of only on fixed reference outputs.

Consider a 50K-token contract task that requires six clauses. One rollout writes a fluent answer with five clauses. Another is awkward but includes all six. The first can look better token by token because every sentence is locally plausible. A verifier that checks coverage should prefer the second.

Group-Calibrated On-Policy Distillation, or GC-OPD, treats this as a disagreement problem. For a group of student rollouts, it computes:

residual = normalized verifier reward - normalized teacher score

If teacher and verifier rank a response similarly, the correction is small. If the teacher overrates an incomplete response, the residual is negative. If the verifier recognizes task completion that the teacher underweights, it is positive. Subtracting the teacher score matters because simply adding verifier reward can reinforce a preference the teacher already expressed.

The response-level residual still has to reach individual tokens. GC-OPD distributes it using bounded weights derived from each token's relative teacher advantage, while preserving the original dense distillation signal. Those weights allocate correction. They do not identify which token is objectively correct.

In one multi-table extraction diagnostic, pairwise teacher-verifier disagreement rose from 40.6% below 8K tokens to 64.0% at 32-64K. Across five long-context benchmarks, the Qwen3-8B average moved from 43.56 with vanilla OPD to 44.65 with GC-OPD under the same setup.

NexusRAG: Your RAG system with knowledge graphs and citation annotations
Check out this production-grade open-source hybrid RAG system that brings together vector retrieval, knowledge graphs (LightRAG), and agent conversations. What makes it special? End-to-end citation tracking and multimodal understanding. Plus, you can switch between cloud (Gemini) and local (Ollama) models without any hassle, and it even works completely offline.

Architecture Highlights (Going Beyond Traditional RAG):
Deep Analysis: Uses Docling or Marker to keep all the important stuff like headers, page numbers, formulas, and layout intact. Say goodbye to the âlosing structureâ problem that traditional RAG systems have.

Dual-Mode Embedding: BGE-M3 handles the fast vector retrieval, while a separate large-dimensional model (Gemini 3072d / local model) takes care of semantic extraction for the knowledge graph.

Hybrid Retrieval: It runs vector pre-fetching (Top 20) and knowledge graph entity matching at the same time, then a cross-encoder does the fine-grained re-ranking. This gives way better accuracy than just using cosine similarity.

Structured Context: Instead of just throwing text together, it puts together KG insights, cited blocks, and related charts in a structured way before feeding them to the LLM.

CAPTCHA, explained : how a checkbox knows you're human.

The "I'm not a robot" box is not a test you pass by clicking it. From the moment the page loads it is already scoring you, and it looks at four kinds of thing: your cookies and session history, what your browser itself looks like, your network, and how your pointer actually moved on the way over.

Real hands wander, hesitate and overshoot. A script goes in a straight line, at a constant speed, into the exact centre.

That score is decided before you ever click. reCAPTCHA v3 hands the site a number from 0.0 to 1.0, and the documented default line is 0.5. Clear it and you are waved through and never see a thing. Fall short and you get the pictures.

Which is why a real person on a private browser with no history gets the traffic lights too. The score is a guess, and it is wrong in both directions.

Ever been called a robot by a website? Save this for the next time you are clicking fire hydrants.

The paddle in this animation cannot push a ball sideways. It can only choose where the ball lands on it. That is the hard part.

The concept is underactuation: you have fewer controls than the directions you need to move things. Most real machines are like this â a car can't slide sideways into a parking spot, and this paddle can't shove a ball left.

What you're watching: two balls fall under gravity onto one paddle that slides along a horizontal rail. The paddle's top is domed, not flat. At each contact the agent â the thing making decisions â picks two numbers: where on the rail to be, and how fast to strike upward.

That's it. Sideways aim is a side effect. Hit a ball off-centre on the dome and it reflects off at an angle, like a tennis ball off a shoulder rather than a racket face.

The score, the reward the agent learns to maximise, is simply how many catches in a row before a ball hits the floor. Two balls, one paddle, so every strike also has to buy time for the other ball.

Takeaway: when you're short an actuator, aim lives in geometry and timing, not in extra motors.

Reference: Tedrake, Underactuated Robotics (MIT, underactuated.mit.edu); Sutton & Barto, Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, for the reward-maximising setup.

SpaceXAI shipped five hireable workers for $200 a month, then wrote the catch into its own Grok Bot documentation and left the page up: all five run on one computer, so one sign-in hands the browser session, the files and the command-line credentials to every one of them

the NSA, CISA and the cyber agencies of the UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand had published the opposite instruction 103 days earlier: no broad or unrestricted access, low-risk and non-sensitive work only

i ran four of mine on one account for a week, counting what each could reach: eleven signed-in apps, one browser profile, and deleting a bot left all of it standing

Grok Bot is worth hiring five times over, and you can draw its blast radius before the second one exists:

- sign in for the bot that needs the site, then open the others and see what they reach: that session is theirs the moment it exists
- give each bot its own account on the app, since the docs tell you in writing to stop using separate bots as a security boundary
- put the stop line in the description, as an approval controls the proposed action and leaves whatever already ran where it landed
- cap the spend outside the product, because there is no bot-specific spend cap yet and the audit view of what they did is still coming
- keep the money and the customer replies in your own hands, and let the other four start from scratch each morning on work that cannot bite

one sign-in is also why this pays: five names finish inside your real tools instead of handing you drafts to paste

my take, and it is the uncomfortable one: your real limit on Grok Bot is how many logins you will put on one machine, and the hiring was always the easy half

A developer used Claude Code to create a file-sharing system that can transfer data between two phones using only a screen and a camera, without relying on Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, or any physical connection.

The system works by turning a file into a sequence of animated QR codes displayed on one phoneâs screen, while the second phone scans and reconstructs the data through its camera. It uses fountain codes, where each frame contains a combination of random file segments, allowing the transfer to continue even if some frames are missed.

The project can transfer a 2 MB image at around 129 KB/s. Built in a single night, the tool has also been released as open source.

The idea actually started from a music-related challenge. The developer wanted to avoid streaming limitations and ads while creating a cached web-based MP3 player. While using Claude Code, they needed a way to move tracks between phones without requiring both devices to be connected to the same network.

The solution? Using rapidly changing QR codes as a wireless bridge between devices.

Hereâs how to make your storytelling so addictive, it is scientifically impossible to skip.

This is called the Dopamine Addiction Loop.

Itâs only 4 steps, but it uses the exact same psychology casinos use to keep you gambling.

Step 1 is the Stakes.

To have any dopamine release, the viewer has to care about the story in the first place.

To get them to care, you need stakes.

Stakes are:

1. A character someone can root for
2. Something at risk
3. Urgency

Step 2 is The Big Question.

This is where you give enough context to have a super juicy question pop in the viewerâs mind.

The stakes make them pay attention, but the big question makes them super curious and locked in.

In the casino, The Big Question when youâre playing Blackjack is which card is going to come next.

Step 3 is the Headfake.

And this is really where you hook them.

The headfake is where you contrast against what the normal viewer should believe.

Lastly, step 4 is the Rehook.

Just like a casino tries to redeal the next Blackjack hand as soon as possible, you want your stories to restart this loop again as quickly as you can.

Good stories have one addiction loop.

Great stories have many cascading throughout.

This combination of Stakes, The Big Question, The Headfake and The Rehook is all you need to tell a super addicting story.

Not all literature reviews serve the same purpose and choosing the wrong one can weaken your entire research.

One of the most common mistakes I see among students and early-career researchers is treating every literature review as if itâs the same.

The truth is, your research objective should determine the type of literature review you choose.

ð Hereâs a simple way to think about it:

ð¹ Narrative Review â Best for providing a broad understanding of a topic.

ð¹ Systematic Literature Review (SLR) â Ideal when you need a structured, transparent, and reproducible synthesis of evidence.

ð¹ Scoping Review â Perfect for exploring emerging fields, identifying research gaps, and mapping existing evidence.

ð¹ Integrative Review â Combines findings from different research methodologies to provide a comprehensive perspective.

ð¹ Theoretical Review â Focuses on theories, models, and conceptual frameworks rather than empirical findings.

ð¹ Critical Review â Goes beyond summarizing literature by evaluating strengths, limitations, and inconsistencies.

ð¹ Meta-analysis â Statistically combines results from multiple quantitative studies to produce stronger evidence.

ð¹ Meta-synthesis â Integrates findings from qualitative studies to generate deeper insights.

ð¹ Rapid Review â A faster approach designed for policy-making and time-sensitive decisions.

ð¹ Umbrella Review â Synthesizes evidence from multiple systematic reviews, offering the highest level of evidence in many fields.

ð Remember: The best literature review isnât the most complex one

itâs the one that aligns with your research question, objectives, and methodology.

Inferno
By Herri met de Bles (16th century)
Palazzo Ducale (Dogeâs Palace), Venice

Not a painting of Hell. A painting that feels like you have already entered it. An enormous dark sphere fills the sky, blotting out anything above â there is no heaven to look up to here, only a ceiling. Along the horizon every city burns. In the centre, naked figures crowd around a red structure and wait, while others are already inside, packed behind a spiked gate. They are not being tortured. They are being processed. On the left, a monk and a nun haul a cart under a demonâs whip: Bles putting the clergy in Hell and making them carry the weight of everyone they failed. And in a bed, a man and a woman lie under the covers with a demon leaning over them and a frog squatting on the blanket â in the sixteenth century, the frog meant lust. Their private sin, made permanent and public.

Context: "My dogmatic slumber was interrupted..." â Immanuel Kant

For years, Immanuel Kant pursued his philosophical inquiries within the comfortable framework of traditional rationalism, convinced that human reason alone could unlock the ultimate truths of metaphysics. He moved through the academic world of KÃ¶nigsberg with methodical precision, holding a firm belief in necessary truths and the innate architecture of the mind. However, this intellectual tranquility was abruptly shattered when he came across the skeptical writings of the Scottish philosopher David Hume. Humeâs rigorous critique, particularly his bold assertion that cause and effect relationships are merely habits of observation rather than objectively demonstrable truths, struck at the very foundation of Kant's worldview.

Reading Hume's essays between 1769 and 1772 acted as a sudden intellectual jolt, pulling Kant out of his long standing conceptual comfort zone. Rather than falling into total skepticism, Kant channeled this shock into a revolutionary paradigm shift. Realizing that reason could no longer be taken for granted without questioning its own limits, he set out to dismantle and rebuild the foundations of epistemology itself. This intense period of reorientation paved the way for his monumental Critique of Pure Reason, forever altering the landscape of modern philosophy.

Wolff's Division of the Sciences: A Historical Philosophical Framework
This academic diagram, titled "Wolff's Division of the Sciences," illustrates the systematic classification of human knowledge proposed by the influential German Enlightenment philosopher Christian Wolff. Rooted in the 18th-century rationalist tradition, this hierarchical tree breaks down all intellectual disciplines into a structured, logical order originating from Knowledge.
Core Branches of Knowledge
At the highest level, knowledge is divided into three primary categories: History (fact), Philosophy (reason of the fact), and Mathematics (quantity of things). The bulk of the diagram focuses on Philosophy, which Wolff subdivides into two major domains: "of things" (theoretical philosophy) and "of human actions" (practical philosophy).
1. Philosophy of Things (Theoretical Knowledge)
This branch is further split into two key areas:
 * Metaphysics (Pneumatics): Encompasses Ontology (being in general), Natural Theology (God), Psychology (human souls), and General Cosmology (world in general). Together, these study abstract and spiritual realities.
 * Physics (Bodies): Covers empirical and natural sciences, branching into General physics (affections of bodies), Cosmology (world as such), Meteorology (atmospheric phenomena), Oryctology (minerals), Hydrology (water), Phytology (plants), Physiology (animated bodies), and Teleology (final causes of natural things).
2. Philosophy of Human Actions (Practical Knowledge)
This domain deals with human agency, logic, and societal organization, categorized under three headings:
 * Cognitive: Focuses on mental processes, including Logic (direction of mind to truth) and Ars inveniendi (discovery of latent truth).
 * Appetitive: Pertains to morality and societal structures, featuring Jus naturae (knowledge of good and evil), Universal practical philosophy, Ethics (individual morality), Politics (civil society), and Oeconomica (lesser societies/households).
 * Productive and Technology: Covers practical arts and communication, including Grammatical, Rhetorical, and Poetical philosophy, alongside Technology (agriculture, civil architecture, etc.).

Quantum mechanics is the branch of physics that describes how nature behaves at the smallest scalesâatoms, electrons, photons, and other subatomic particles. Unlike everyday physics (classical mechanics), it reveals a world that behaves in ways that can seem strange or counterintuitive.
ð§  Core Ideas
1. Quantization
Energy doesnât vary continuously at tiny scalesâit comes in discrete âpacketsâ called quanta.
Example: electrons in an atom can only occupy certain energy levels.
2. WaveâParticle Duality
Particles like electrons and photons behave both like particles and waves.
This idea was famously demonstrated in the Double-slit experiment.
3. Uncertainty Principle
Formulated by Werner Heisenberg, it states that certain pairs of properties (like position and momentum) cannot both be known exactly at the same time.
4. Superposition
A quantum system can exist in multiple states at once until it is measured.
A famous illustration is SchrÃ¶dinger's catâa cat that is both alive and dead until observed.
5. Entanglement
Particles can become linked so that the state of one instantly affects the other, even across large distances.
Albert Einstein called this âspooky action at a distance.â
ð¬ Why It Matters
Quantum mechanics underpins much of modern technology:
Semiconductors â computers & smartphones
Lasers â medicine, communications
MRI machines â medical imaging
Quantum computing â next-generation computing
âï¸ Key Figures
Max Planck â introduced the idea of quanta
Niels Bohr â model of the atom
Erwin SchrÃ¶dinger â wave equation
Paul Dirac â unified quantum mechanics and relativity
ð Big Picture
Quantum mechanics doesnât replace classical physicsâit extends it. At large scales, quantum effects average out, and the familiar laws of motion take over. But at the microscopic level, probability, uncertainty, and duality dominate.

A solo developer just got a 744B-parameter GLM MoE model running on a 25GB RAM laptop with no GPU.

The idea is surprisingly simple: instead of loading the entire model into memory, it keeps only the ~9.9GB dense core in RAM and streams the remaining 370GB of expert weights from an SSD on demand, one token at a time.

What used to require datacenter-scale hardware can now run on a consumer laptop.

Highlights:
â¢ Runs a 744B MoE model with ~25GB RAM
â¢ No GPU required
â¢ Written in pure C with zero dependencies
â¢ Single 2,400-line source file
â¢ Apache 2.0 licensed
â¢ 8,000+ GitHub stars in under two weeks

The trade-off? Speed.

Early benchmarks show:
â¢ ~0.05â0.1 tokens/sec on the author's laptop (cold start)
â¢ Faster as the SSD cache warms and speculative decoding kicks in
â¢ Around 1 token/sec on an Apple M5 Max
â¢ Around 0.37 tokens/sec on a Framework 13
â¢ Up to 6.84 tokens/sec across six RTX 5090s

No, this isn't replacing your everyday inference setup anytime soon.

But that's not the point.

The breakthrough is that a 744B frontier-scale MoE model can run on consumer hardware by treating the SSD as an extension of memory. The bottleneck is no longer fitting the model into RAMâit's storage bandwidth.

the best open models have been paywalled by hardware, not price.

llama 3.3 70B is free to download. running it costs 140GB of VRAM, which means students and researchers rent thousand-dollar compute nodes to touch a model that costs nothing.

airllm breaks that math. its an open-source python library (22.4k stars) that runs 70B models on a single 4GB gpu, or a macbook.

how: inference executes a model layer by layer, in order, ~80 layers for a 70B llama. no rule says they all have to sit in memory at once. airllm loads one layer, runs it, dumps it, loads the next. peak VRAM is one layer, about 1.6GB.

nothing is quantized by default, so the output is bit-identical to running the same weights on an A100 node.

the tradeoff: time. every token reads the full model off disk, so expect seconds per token even on fast NVMe. fine for offline jobs and testing 70B output before renting real hardware. not fine for chat.

setup is pip install airllm plus one script. i wrote the whole thing up, disk requirements and all.

A solo dev got GLM-5.2, a 744B-parameter model, running on a 25GB laptop with no GPU.

> no GPU, pure C, zero dependencies, one 2400-line file

The catch is speed, and it is real. Cold, on the authorâs own box, it runs about 0.05 to 0.1 tokens per second. It gets faster as the cache warms and the built-in speculative decoding kicks in, roughly 2 to 3 tokens per forward pass.

The community numbers line up. Around 1 token per second on an Apple M5 Max, 0.37 on a Framework 13, and 6.84 across six RTX 5090s. The reception has been honest everywhere. Tomâs Hardware put it best, âitâs slow, yes, but itâs a start,â and the author says the same thing right in the readme, âthis is not fast.â

TabFM is a zero-shot tabular foundation model from Google Research.

It reads your whole table as context and predicts fraud, churn, and demand from a companyâs tables in one forward pass, no training, no tuning, no feature engineering.

Here: github.com/google-research/tabfm

For years the industry standard for this was highly fine-tuned XGBoost and other tree models. Google says TabFM beats them out of the box, on tables it has never seen before.

And this exact job, predicting fraud, churn, and demand from a companyâs tables, is the core of what Palantir Foundry sells to banks and governments.

To be clear, TabFM is not replacing Palantir. Palantir is a full ecosystem: the data pipeline, the interfaces, the deployment, and a lot more. But at the core, the final prediction and the final output are the same thing, and Google just open sourced that part.

> reads training rows as context, predicts the test rows in a single pass
> classification and regression on mixed number and text columns
> Google says it beats heavily tuned XGBoost on its TabArena benchmark
> trained on hundreds of millions of synthetic tables, not real data
> open weights on HuggingFace, runs from one Python file
> coming to BigQuery as a plain AI.PREDICT SQL command

Teaching methods are planned ways used by teachers to help students learn effectively. Different methods are used for different learning goals.

ð¹ Lecture Method â Teacher explains the topic to many students at once.

ð¹ Discussion Method â Students and teacher share ideas and opinions.

ð¹ Demonstration Method â Learning by watching a process or skill.

ð¹ Project Method â Learning through activities and real-life tasks.

ð¹ Seminar Method â A topic is presented and discussed in detail.

ð¹ Symposium Method â Experts share different views on the same topic.

ð¹ Workshop Method â Hands-on learning through practice.

ð¹ Panel Discussion â Experts discuss a topic before an audience.

ð¹ Role Play Method â Students act out situations to learn concepts.

ð¹ Brainstorming Method â Free sharing of ideas without criticism.

ð¹ Problem Solving Method â Students identify problems and find solutions.

ð¹ Heuristic Method â Learning through self-discovery and exploration.

ð¹ Inductive Method â Learning moves from specific examples to general rules.

ð¹ Deductive Method â Learning moves from general rules to specific examples.

ð¹ Assignment Method â Tasks are given for independent learning and practice.

ð¹ Tutorial Method â Individual or small-group guidance by the teacher.

ð¹ Laboratory Method â Learning through experiments and practical work.

ð¹ Team Teaching â Two or more teachers teach together.

ð¹ Programmed Instruction â Learning in small steps with immediate feedback.

ð¹ Micro Teaching â Practice of one teaching skill at a time.

â­ Key Points:
â No single teaching method is best for every situation.
â Choose methods according to learners, objectives and resources.

Markov Chain âï¸

It explains how systems can evolve step by step, where the next move depends only on the present state and not on the full history. Imagine walking through a maze, flipping between weather conditions, or moving from one webpage to another. At every step, your next destination is chosen by a set of probabilities linked only to where you are right now.

A Markov chain treats each possible situation as a âstateâ and connects them with chances of moving from one state to another. If you are in a sunny state, there may be a high chance of staying sunny and a smaller chance of turning rainy. Once the next step is chosen, the past no longer matters â the system âforgetsâ everything except its current position.

Over many steps, patterns begin to emerge. Some states may appear more often, some may rarely be visited, and in many systems the probabilities settle into a stable long-term balance called the steady-state distribution. This reveals the hidden rhythm beneath seemingly random motion.

Scientists use Markov chains to model weather, genetics, stock markets, search engines, and even language generation. By following these probabilistic transitions, they can predict behavior, analyze uncertainty, and understand how complex systems move through time.#physics #science #fyp #amazing #explore

Metamorphic malware is considered the "holy grail" of evasion in malware development. While polymorphic malware hides its core by encrypting itself and changing its decryption routine each time, metamorphic malware completely rewrites its own body with every iteration. 

The resulting file looks, structurally and binary-wise, 100% different from its parent, yet its functional behavior remains exactly the same.

When the malware infects a system, it reads its own binary code and uses a built-in Disassembler to translate the raw machine code back into assembly language.

It then passes that assembly through a Mutation Engine, which shuffles the logic.

Finally, it uses an internal Assembler/Compiler to rebuild the mutated code back into a brand-new, unique binary executable (.exe or .elf) to infect the next file.

At 22, Alexandra Elbakyan built Sci-Hub, a controversial shadow library that changed how millions of people access scientific research. What started in 2011 as a way around expensive journal paywalls grew into one of the largest archives of academic papers online. Sci-Hub has been called a pirate library because it gives free access to paywalled papers, often without publisher permission. A 2018 eLife study found that Sci-Hub covered 85.1% of toll access journal articles at the time, showing how massive its reach had already become. Now the story has entered the AI era. Sci-Hub has reportedly launched Sci-Bot, an experimental AI research assistant that can answer questions using papers from its archive, though early reports say it still has limits with newer research and deeper follow-up questions. Publishers see Sci-Hub as copyright infringement, and Elsevier previously won a major damages case against the site. Supporters see it as a rebellion against a system where scientific knowledge is often locked behind expensive paywalls.

Dark City (1998) and The Matrix (1999) are foundational sci-fi films sharing concepts of manufactured realities and a protagonist with newly awakened powers. Because both were shot in Australia, the Wachowskis even reused several iconic sets from Dark City to produce The Matrix.

Both feature a city built as a prison/experiment for humanity. In Dark City, an alien race alters the physical city and erases human memories every night to study the human soul. In The Matrix, machines trap humanity in a simulated world to harvest their bioelectric energy.

The single most underused file in agentic coding is one page long.

CLAUDE.md is the brief your agent reads at the start of every session. You write it once â like the README you'd hand a new teammate on day one. Five sections, under 150 lines.

Without it: every new session, your agent lists files, reads package.json, greps for the test runner. Three round-trips before the first useful edit.

With it: the agent opens the file, sees your stack, jumps straight to the fix.

The five sections that earn their place: Commands (exact build/test/lint), Architecture (where routes and DB live), Hard rules (mark IMPORTANT), Workflow preferences (minimal diffs, ask before destructive ops), Out of scope (what the agent should never touch).

Keep it under 150 lines â past that, your rules get lost. And keep it alive: type # then your rule mid-task, and the agent writes it to the file for you.

Save this for the next time you start a new agent project.

Visualizing LLaMA 3.2 LLM helps make its behavior more intuitive: each token is turned into a high-dimensional vector, and layers of connections transform these vectors as they pass through the network.

Attention patterns can be viewed as grids showing how strongly each token attends to others, revealing relationships like grammar and context between words.

Together, these connections determine how the model predicts the next token, with different pathways activating depending on the input sequence.

During training, backpropagation adjusts these connections by looking at large amounts of text data, nudging parameters (in which the matrix multiplication represents the connections of the network) so that useful token relationships are strengthened and less useful ones are weakened.

Over time, this process shapes the network into a system that can generate coherent and language by coordinating attention and learned transformations across its layers.

Leslie Lamport is a computer scientist who won the 2013 Turing Award, often called the Nobel Prize of computing. He's best known for creating LaTeX, the typesetting system used in virtually every academic paper worldwide, and for foundational work in distributed systems that powers companies like Amazon, Microsoft, and Intel. Before his work, engineers had no reliable way to make multiple computers coordinate without catastrophic errors. His algorithms (Paxos, Lamport clocks) became the invisible backbone of modern cloud infrastructure.

His core argument about programming education is deceptively simple: learning to code without learning to think mathematically is like learning to type without learning to write. He created TLA+, a formal specification language that forces engineers to define what a program is supposed to do, the logic, the edge cases, the mathematical proof of correctness, before writing a single line of code. AWS adopted TLA+ internally and credited it with catching critical bugs that traditional testing missed entirely. The catch is that most engineers resist it because it requires the kind of mathematical thinking that, as Lamport bluntly puts it, the education system has made people afraid of. His method isn't about writing better code. It's about thinking clearly enough that the code almost writes itself

Inside your smartphone there is a hidden system most people never think about. Itâs called the baseband processor. This is the chip responsible for handling cellular communication â calls, SMS, 4G, 5G, and constant communication with nearby cell towers.
Unlike apps or the operating system, the baseband runs independently and is always active as long as your phone has signal.
Hereâs where it gets interesting.
Your phone constantly receives low-level network messages from cell towers: registration updates, handover commands, signaling packets, and other control data. The baseband firmware parses and processes these messages automatically.
If there is a vulnerability in how the baseband handles certain malformed or specially crafted packets, an attacker could exploit it. By sending a malicious cellular signal or manipulating network signaling traffic, the attacker may trigger memory corruption inside the baseband firmware. In advanced scenarios, this can lead to remote code execution.
That means code could run inside the cellular processor without the user clicking anything â no link, no download, no interaction.
In extremely rare but high-impact cases, researchers have demonstrated that baseband exploits could potentially allow:
Intercepting communications
Tracking device identifiers
Disrupting cellular connectivity
Or pivoting toward the main operating system
These attacks are highly sophisticated and usually require deep telecom knowledge or access to specialized infrastructure. They are not typical âscript-kiddieâ hacks.
The key takeaway:
Your phone has multiple layers. Even if you never open a suspicious app, the cellular layer is still exposed to network signals at all times.
This is why keeping your device updated matters â baseband firmware updates are often included in system security patches, even if you never see them.
